sections.evidence: Robert A. Wagner and Michael J. Fischer's 1974 paper The String-to-String Correction Problem is one of the foundational algorithmic papers in the modern history of edit distance.
paragraphs: Robert A. Wagner and Michael J. Fischer's 1974 paper The String-to-String Correction Problem is one of the foundational algorithmic papers in the modern history of edit distance.
Its importance is often summarized in a single sentence:
It gives the classic O(mn) dynamic-programming algorithm for edit distance.
That statement is correct, but it understates the paper.

Wagner and Fischer do not begin by writing down a three-way recurrence and declaring it obvious. They first define a general weighted theory of edit operations, reduce arbitrary edit sequences to order-preserving structures they call traces , prove that minimum edit-sequence cost equals minimum trace cost, derive the dynamic-programming recurrence from the structure of an optimal trace, give an explicit algorithm for computing the distance, give a second algorithm for recovering a minimum-cost trace, prove the traceback algorithm correct, and finally show how the same framework computes a longest common subsequence.
The paper therefore establishes a complete chain:

edit operations | v edit sequences | v traces | v minimum-cost trace theorem | v optimal substructure | v dynamic-programming recurrence | v O(mn) algorithm | v traceback | v longest common subsequence.
It also works with substantially more general edit costs than the unit-cost version typically taught as the Levenshtein distance algorithm.

The original article appeared in the Journal of the ACM , volume 21, issue 1, pages 168–173, in January 1974, with DOI 10.1145/321796.321811 . The manuscript records that it was received in February 1972 and revised in March 1973.

This page analyzes the paper itself: its definitions, assumptions, proofs, algorithms, complexity, relation to Levenshtein distance, relation to longest common subsequence, and the boundary between what Wagner and Fischer actually proved and what later literature added.

sections.heading: 468. Final interpretation
sections.evidence: The String-to-String Correction Problem is best understood as the paper that turns a general theory of character edits into a complete dynamic-programming framework.
paragraphs: The String-to-String Correction Problem is best understood as the paper that turns a general theory of character edits into a complete dynamic-programming framework.
The starting point is deliberately broad.
Wagner and Fischer do not assume that every edit costs one. They define a nonnegative real cost:
for changing, deleting, or inserting individual symbols, and define:
as the minimum total cost of any edit sequence transforming A into B .
This means the paper's true subject is not merely unit-cost Levenshtein distance. It is a weighted string-to-string correction problem in which the application determines the local cost model.
The key theoretical move is the trace.
An arbitrary edit history can be complicated:
change a character change it again delete another character insert something modify an inserted character ...
Such histories are difficult to optimize over directly.
The trace strips them down to what matters:
which source positions survive into which target positions which source positions are deleted which target positions are inserted.
The correspondence must be order preserving. Trace lines cannot cross because the operation set contains no reordering primitive.
Wagner and Fischer then prove two complementary properties:
every trace can be realized by an equal-cost edit sequence and every edit sequence can be compressed into a trace of no greater cost.
minimum edit-sequence cost = minimum trace cost.
This is Theorem 1, and it is the conceptual foundation of the dynamic program.
Once the optimization problem has been reduced to traces, the famous recurrence becomes unavoidable.
an optimal trace can end in only three ways:
A(i) paired with B(j) A(i) deleted B(j) inserted.
The corresponding boundary values are the costs of deleting or inserting entire prefixes.

The resulting paper architecture is remarkably complete:

GENERAL EDIT COSTS | v EDIT SEQUENCES | v TRACES | v NORMAL-FORM THEOREM | v PREFIX OPTIMAL SUBSTRUCTURE | v THREE-WAY RECURRENCE | v ALGORITHM X O(mn) | v ALGORITHM Y TRACEBACK | v LCS SPECIALIZATION.
Just as important are the boundaries of the 1974 result.

It does not include adjacent transposition. It does not include affine gap penalties. It does not implement local alignment. It does not provide a bounded k-band algorithm. It does not use bit parallelism. It does not provide a corpus indexing strategy. It does not make arbitrary weighted costs automatically metric. It does not claim the minimum edit path is the real physical history of the strings.
Those developments belong to later research.

Lowrance and Wagner added adjacent swapping in 1975. Masek and Paterson pursued faster exact computation. Ukkonen exploited small edit distance and bounded thresholds. Myers represented dynamic-programming state with machine-word bit vectors. Levenshtein automata compiled bounded edit neighborhoods into finite-state recognizers. Filtering and indexing methods turned pairwise verification into scalable search.
Yet these later techniques continue to orbit the same basic recurrence because Wagner and Fischer captured the essential optimal substructure so cleanly.
The paper's enduring contribution can therefore be summarized not as:

a proof that minimum-cost string correction can be reduced to an order-preserving positional structure whose optimum decomposes over prefixes and therefore admits quadratic-time dynamic programming plus exact traceback.
That result became one of the canonical examples of dynamic programming in computer science and the computational foundation for one of the most widely used sequence distances in modern software.
